summary:
We built Skyshift, a website that lets people compare infrared pictures of the same part of the sky taken on different dates.

Users can enter an object’s coordinates, choose an example, or upload a list of observations. Skyshift finds suitable images, lines them up, and creates a timeline so users can look for changes or movement.

Our example is Epsilon Indi B, a nearby brown-dwarf system. We see a possible shift between images, but it still needs checking before we can confidently call it measured movement.

The code is now on GitHub, and you have connected it to Render, which will run the website online.

Next, finish the Render settings and click Deploy web service. Once it succeeds, Render will give you a public link that anyone can open.
details:
Skyshift turns infrared astronomy data into a visual timeline, helping people explore how objects in space appear to change over time.

Users enter sky coordinates, choose an example, or upload an observation list. Skyshift checks SPHEREx image metadata, selects observations at similar wavelengths, and downloads small image sections. It aligns them to the same sky view, marks missing or questionable pixels, and displays a comparison or animation.

Our demonstration uses Epsilon Indi B, a nearby brown-dwarf system. It compares image-based position estimates with catalog predictions while clearly distinguishing preliminary measurements from expected movement.

The intended impact is to make NASA data easier for students, citizen scientists, and researchers to explore. Skyshift supports visual investigation of moving objects, a useful starting point for searches involving nearby, faint objects.

We built it using Python, FastAPI, Astropy, NumPy, pandas, SciPy, Matplotlib, and reproject, with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the interface. We used Google Colab for exploration, GitHub for code, and Docker for deployment.

Our creative approach combines complex scientific files with an accessible timeline. We considered limited time, download sizes, wavelength differences, image quality, and the importance of avoiding unsupported scientific claims.
